title: Non-medical sex selection in IVF
short_description: An IVF clinic must decide whether embryo sex may guide transfer when sex is already known from PGT-A, no medical indication exists, and a patient requests selection for family balancing.
decision_question: What policy should an IVF clinic use for embryo sex selection when no sex-linked disease or other medical indication is present?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral fertility-clinic policy; permissive and restrictive non-medical sex-selection policies are stipulated to be legally available.

stipulations.statement: The patient is already undergoing IVF for an independent clinical reason rather than initiating IVF solely for sex selection.
stipulations.rationale: This removes the additional medical burdens of starting IVF solely for non-medical selection from the policy comparison.

stipulations.statement: Embryo sex is already known from PGT-A and no additional biopsy or testing is required solely for sex selection.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark isolates use of already-generated sex information in transfer choice.

stipulations.statement: No sex-linked disease or other medical indication for sex selection is present.
stipulations.rationale: Medically indicated sex selection is a different and substantially less contested policy question.

stipulations.statement: The patient has two healthy children of the same sex and requests transfer of an otherwise suitable embryo of the other sex for family balancing.
stipulations.rationale: The fixed request lies where permissive and restrictive clinic policies diverge while avoiding a generic preference with no family context.

stipulations.statement: Both permitting and declining non-medical sex selection are legally available to the clinic.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests ethical clinic policy rather than jurisdiction-specific law.

position_families: decline non-medical use of embryo sex

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored clinic-policy representation grounded in ASRM and ESHRE professional ethics guidance and public-attitude evidence. It fixes independent IVF, already-known embryo sex, absence of medical indication and a family-balancing request so the executable candidates differ on clinic participation.

public.text: Allow patients already undergoing IVF to use embryo sex as a transfer preference for family balancing after counseling, provided the choice is voluntary and does not displace a medically superior embryo.

provenance.summary: Adapted from population evidence of a minority permissive orientation, cited directly rather than through a professional body’s summary. Dahl found 8% of US adults would use preconception sex selection while 50% wished for an equal number of boys and girls — the family-balancing interest this candidate serves — and Winkelman found 21.1% of a nationally representative sample supported PGD for sex selection. The candidate represents that minority position and the clinic permission rule and medical-priority safeguard are Bench-authored; it is not a claim of majority support.

sources.citation: Dahl E, Gupta RS, Beutel M, Stoebel-Richter Y, Brosig B, Tinneberg HR, et al. Preconception sex selection demand and preferences in the United States. Fertil Steril. 2006;85(2):468-73. Survey of 1,197 US adults aged 18-45: 8% would use preconception sex selection, 74% were opposed, and 50% wished for a family with an equal number of boys and girls. PMID 16595229.

Winkelman WD, Missmer SA, Myers D, Ginsburg ES. Public perspectives on the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis. J Assist Reprod Genet. 2015;32(5):665-75. Nationally representative US sample of 1,006 adults; 21.1% supported PGD for sex selection, against 72.9% supporting PGD for diseases fatal early in life. PMID 25758988.
Dahl E, Hinsch KD, Brosig B, Beutel M. Attitudes towards preconception sex selection: a representative survey from Germany. Reprod Biomed Online. 2004;9(6):600-3. PMID 15670402.

public.text: Do not allow embryo sex to determine transfer when no medical indication exists, even when the request is for family balancing and sex information is already available.

provenance.summary: Adapted from population evidence of majority opposition, cited directly rather than through a professional body’s summary. Dahl found 74% of US adults opposed to preconception sex selection; Kippen found high and rising Australian disapproval of IVF sex selection including for family balancing, which is this scenario’s exact request; Winkelman’s 21.1% support for PGD sex selection is the same finding from the other side. The clinic policy of declining, disclosing and applying consistently is a Bench translation of that orientation.

sources.citation: Dahl E, Gupta RS, Beutel M, Stoebel-Richter Y, Brosig B, Tinneberg HR, et al. Preconception sex selection demand and preferences in the United States. Fertil Steril. 2006;85(2):468-73. Survey of 1,197 US adults aged 18-45: 8% would use preconception sex selection, 74% were opposed, and 50% wished for a family with an equal number of boys and girls. PMID 16595229.

Kippen R, Gray E, Evans A. High and growing disapproval of sex-selection technology in Australia. Reprod Health. 2018;15(1):134. Australian Survey of Social Attitudes, 2007 and 2016; disapproval of IVF sex selection, including for family balancing, is high and rose across the two waves. PMID 30185179.

Winkelman WD, Missmer SA, Myers D, Ginsburg ES. Public perspectives on the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis. J Assist Reprod Genet. 2015;32(5):665-75. Nationally representative US sample of 1,006 adults; 21.1% supported PGD for sex selection, against 72.9% supporting PGD for diseases fatal early in life. PMID 25758988.

expert.text: Permit a clinic to provide non-medical embryo sex selection for a patient already undergoing IVF, including family balancing, after informed counseling about medical burdens, coercion, stereotyping and social-justice concerns and under a transparent written clinic policy.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ASRM 2022, which says practitioners are under no ethical obligation to refuse non-medical sex selection, identifies reproductive-liberty arguments, and requires clinics to develop transparent policies and address relevant risks. The detailed safeguards operationalize the opinion for this scenario.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Use of reproductive technology for sex selection for nonmedical reasons: an Ethics Committee opinion. Fertility and Sterility. 2022;117:720-726.

expert.text: Adopt a clinic policy declining embryo sex as a transfer criterion unless sex selection is medically indicated, disclose that policy before treatment, and apply it consistently.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ASRM 2022, which says practitioners are under no ethical obligation to provide non-medical sex selection, states that the practice should not be encouraged, and identifies discrimination, stereotyping and justice concerns as legitimate grounds for a clinic policy.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Use of reproductive technology for sex selection for nonmedical reasons: an Ethics Committee opinion. Fertility and Sterility. 2022;117:720-726.

framework.text: Permit the family-balancing request because choosing among otherwise suitable embryos can be part of reproductive liberty and the request need not express unequal valuation of either sex.

provenance.summary: Derived from reproductive-liberty reasoning and the distinction between family balancing and categorical preference for one sex. The executable policy is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Use of reproductive technology for sex selection for nonmedical reasons. 2022.
Dondorp W, et al. ESHRE Task Force on Ethics and Law 20: sex selection for non-medical reasons. Human Reproduction. 2013;28:1448-1454.

framework.text: Decline the family-balancing request because clinic participation in non-medical sex selection can reinforce sex stereotyping, unequal valuation and expectations that constrain children's open futures and wider equality.

provenance.summary: Derived from anti-discrimination, social-justice and open-future reasoning. The executable policy is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Use of reproductive technology for sex selection for nonmedical reasons. 2022.

scenario: A fertility clinic routinely performs IVF with PGT-A. For this benchmark, assume the patient is already undergoing IVF for an independent clinical reason, has two healthy children of the same sex, requests transfer of an otherwise suitable embryo of the other sex for family balancing, embryo sex is already known from PGT-A with no additional biopsy or testing required, no sex-linked disease or other medical indication exists, no coercion is identified, and both permitting and declining non-medical selection are legally available. The clinic is concerned both with reproductive choice and with sex stereotyping, discrimination and the social meaning of clinical participation. It must choose a standing policy governing whether embryo sex may guide transfer in this family-balancing circumstance.
